summary:
FireBridge: Harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS Fire Records

NASA's MODIS sensors (Terra and Aqua) have detected active fires since 2000 with ~1 km pixels. VIIRS on Suomi NPP joined in 2012 with 375 m pixels and sees many more, smaller fires. Joining the two records makes fire activity seem to jump in 2012, hiding real trends.

FireBridge learns how the sensors differ from years they both observed and rebuilds 2000–2012 on the VIIRS scale. NASA FIRMS vegetation-fire detections are gridded into 10 km cells per month; an XGBoost model adjusts each region's VIIRS/MODIS ratio using MODIS fire power, pixel size, nearby fires and season. A 5-model ensemble gives an uncertainty band.

Results in 8 regions with different fire types (savanna, boreal and Mediterranean forest, bushfire, wetland, peat, crop burning, shrubland):
• The fake 2012 jump disappears in all 8.
• On 2022–2025, never used for training: 11.1% monthly error, +1.4% total bias.
• Known events stand out, e.g. Australia 2019, Pantanal 2020, Canada 2023.

A live web app shows each region's burning-activity calendar, fire map and model scores.

Impact: one consistent 25-year fire record, so researchers, land managers and responders can compare fire activity across years and places.

Limitation: accuracy drops for fire types the model has never seen.
details:
What FireBridge does

NASA has watched fires from space with MODIS (Terra and Aqua satellites, ~1 km pixels) since 2000, and with VIIRS (Suomi NPP satellite, 375 m pixels) since 2012. VIIRS sees much more: one fire can become several VIIRS detections, and small fires MODIS misses become visible. Joining the two records therefore creates a jump in 2012 that never happened. In Egypt's Nile Delta the joined record rises 9.4×, while the real change, measured by MODIS alone, was 1.2×. FireBridge removes that jump and gives one consistent fire record from 2000 to today, shown as a burning-activity calendar for each region.

How it works

1. Data: we download NASA FIRMS active-fire detections for 8 study regions with very different fires: savanna burning (Guinea), Mediterranean forest (Portugal), boreal forest (Canada), bushfires (Australia), wetland fires (Brazil's Pantanal), peat fires (Indonesia), rice-straw burning (Egypt's Nile Delta) and shrubland and dry forest fires (Argentina's La Rioja). We keep vegetation fires only and remove gas flares and industrial heat sources.

2. Grid: every detection is placed on an equal-area grid of 10 × 10 km cells and counted per month, so MODIS and VIIRS can be compared cell by cell.

3. Model: for each region we start from the ratio of VIIRS to MODIS detections, then an XGBoost model (Poisson loss) learns how much to adjust it in each cell and month, using only what MODIS saw: fire radiative power, pixel size, fires in neighbouring cells, the cell's history and the season. Because the model only corrects the ratio, record fire months still scale with MODIS instead of being capped.

4. Rebuild the past: the model is applied to 2000–2012, when only MODIS existed, to estimate what VIIRS would have seen. From 2013 the calendar shows real VIIRS. Five models trained on different samples give an uncertainty band.

5. Honest testing: the data is split by year, never at random. We train on 2013–2020, tune on 2021 and score once on 2022–2025, years the model never saw.

Results

- The fake 2012 jump disappears in all 8 regions: the harmonized change matches the real change measured by MODIS alone (for example Portugal 0.78× vs 0.75×, Guinea 0.98× vs 0.98×).

- On 2022–2025: 11.1% monthly error per region, +1.4% total bias, 0.99 correlation, and 5× lower error per 10 km cell than a simple ratio.

- Documented fires stand out as the most unusual months in their regions: Australia's Black Summer (November 2019), Portugal's June and October 2017 fires, Canada's 2023 record season and the 2020 Pantanal fires.

Benefits and intended impact

- Researchers can measure real long-term fire trends across the 2012 sensor switch instead of an artefact of better satellites.

- Land managers can compare this season with 25 years of history in the same units, cell by cell.

- Emergency planners can see when a month is truly unusual for its region.

- The method is open and reproducible, so it can be extended to any region on Earth.

The web app (firebridge-brown.vercel.app)

- Calendar: a burning-activity calendar per region that switches between the harmonized record, the raw join, MODIS and VIIRS, with known events outlined, yearly trends, test scores and the most unusual months.

- Fire map: fire detections per 10 km cell for any year and month, and a custom area you draw yourself.

- Analytics and Model pages: how the regions differ and how the model works.

- Downloads: data as CSV and charts as PNG, with colour-blind-safe colour scales.

Tools, languages and software

- Data source: NASA FIRMS (MODIS Collection 6.1, VIIRS S-NPP 375 m; yearly archives plus the FIRMS Area API for the current year).

- Data and machine learning: Python, Google Colab Pro (CPU for data, GPU for training), Google Drive, Parquet, DuckDB, pandas, NumPy, XGBoost, scikit-learn, Matplotlib.

- Web: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, Leaflet; hosted on Vercel; code on GitHub.

- An AI coding assistant (Claude) helped with code, testing and documentation; the team chose the challenge, regions, method and checks, and reviewed the results.

- No special hardware: everything runs in the browser and in free or low-cost cloud notebooks.

What makes it creative

- Instead of matching single fire detections, we model counts per cell and month, which lets the model add back the small fires MODIS never saw (in the Nile Delta, 88% of VIIRS detections had no MODIS detection nearby).

- "Ratio × learned correction": a simple physical baseline plus machine learning only for what the ratio gets wrong.

- Validation with real events: besides test scores, the calendar has to show known disasters and not the sensor switch.

- The burning-activity calendar turns 25 years of satellite data into one picture anyone can read.

Factors our team considered

- Honest evaluation: split by year, test years scored once, overlapping areas removed so no region leaks into another's test, and a leave-one-region-out test that shows our main limitation (fire types the model has never seen are predicted poorly).

- Data quality: gas flares removed (also in near-real-time data, where FIRMS doesn't label them), download gaps detected and retried, unfinished months left out instead of shown as quiet months.

- Scale and cost: data stored as Parquet and processed with DuckDB so it runs within Colab's memory; the app needs no server, so it stays fast and free to host.

- Trust and accessibility: model estimates are labelled as estimates, uncertainty is shown, colour scales include colour-blind-safe options, and the FIRMS key is kept on the server.
